questions.topic: One-to-one functions and the horizontal line test
questions.learningObjective: state the horizontal line test for one-to-one behaviour
questions.stem: A function f is one-to-one on a stated interval exactly when which condition holds on that interval?

options.text: Every horizontal line crosses the graph of f at most once
Every vertical line crosses the graph of f at most once
options.misconception: confuses the horizontal line test with the vertical line test, which only certifies that f is a function

options.text: The graph of f passes through the point of origin exactly once
options.misconception: believes a function is one-to-one only if it starts at the origin

options.text: Every straight line crosses the graph of f at most twice
options.misconception: assumes a fixed bound of two intersections, which no test of one-to-one behaviour requires

questions.explanation: One-to-one means no two distinct inputs share an output, so a horizontal line, which holds one output value fixed, may meet the graph in at most one place. The vertical line test is a different question: it checks that no input has two outputs, which is what makes the relation a function at all, and a function like f(x) = x squared passes that test while failing the horizontal one. No bound on the number of intersections with an arbitrary straight line is involved, and the origin plays no part.
questions.hint: A horizontal line fixes the output, so count how many inputs can produce it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: One-to-one functions and the horizontal line test
questions.learningObjective: explain why a symmetric graph cannot be one-to-one and what restriction repairs it
questions.stem: The function f(x) = x squared is not one-to-one on the whole real line. What is the structural reason, and what fixes it?

options.text: Its graph is symmetric about the y-axis, and restricting to a half-line where x squared is strictly monotone repairs it
Its graph is symmetric about the y-axis, and restricting to the open interval from minus 1 to 1 repairs it
options.misconception: restricts to a window straddling the vertex, where x squared rises and then falls, so the symmetry survives

options.text: Its graph is unbounded above, and only bounded functions can be inverted on an interval
options.misconception: believes one-to-one behaviour requires a bounded output, which polynomial growth on a half-line disproves

options.text: Its graph has a horizontal tangent at the origin, and any critical point prevents an inverse existing
options.misconception: believes a stationary point blocks an inverse, ignoring that f(x) = x cubed has a stationary point and an inverse

questions.explanation: The symmetry is the whole story. Whenever a graph carries a point whose mirror image across the y-axis is also on the graph, two different inputs share one output, so the horizontal line through that height meets the graph twice. On the closed half-line from 0 upward the function x squared is strictly increasing, so no such pair survives; a window centred on the vertex keeps both branches and therefore keeps the collision. A vertical tangent or a critical point is irrelevant here, since x cubed is strictly increasing on all of the real line despite being flat at 0.
questions.hint: Look for two different inputs producing the same height, then cut the domain so only one remains.

questions.topic: One-to-one functions and the horizontal line test
questions.learningObjective: use the discriminant to count real solutions of a parameter-dependent quadratic
questions.stem: For how many real values of the parameter k does the equation x^2 = 6x - 5 + k have exactly one real solution? Report that value of k.
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives the quadratic x^2 - 6x + 5 - k = 0, whose discriminant is 36 minus 4 times 5 minus k, that is 16 plus 4k. Exactly one real solution means the discriminant is exactly zero, so 16 plus 4k = 0 and k = -4. The same answer falls out of the vertex picture: the parabola in x has its minimum at x = 3, where its value is 9 - 18 + 5 - k, that is -4 - k; the graph grazes the x-axis only when that minimum is zero, again k = -4. For k above -4 there are two real solutions, and for k below -4 there are none.
questions.hint: One real solution means the discriminant is zero, so set 16 + 4k equal to zero.

questions.learningObjective: describe what happens to the domain and the range when a function is inverted
questions.stem: If a function f is one-to-one on a domain D with range R, what are the domain and range of its inverse?

options.text: The inverse has domain R and range D, so the two are exchanged exactly
The inverse has domain D and range R, unchanged from the original function
options.misconception: assumes the domain and range survive inversion untouched, ignoring the exchange of roles

options.text: The inverse has domain R and range R, since the range is the only set that matters
options.misconception: sends the range to itself, forgetting that outputs become inputs on inversion

options.text: The inverse has domain D and range D, since one-to-one behaviour is self-referential
options.misconception: believes injectivity forces the domain to equal the range

questions.hint: An inverse is meant to be evaluated on what the original function produced.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why an inverse graph is the reflection of the original in the line y equals x
questions.stem: Explain in a few sentences why the graph of an inverse is the mirror image of the original graph in the line y equals x.

answer.exemplar: A point (a, b) on the graph of f means that f(a) = b, that is, b = f(a). Swapping the two coordinates gives the point (b, a), and reading the pair in the original order says a = f(b), i.e. f(b) = a, which is exactly the statement that (b, a) lies on the graph of the inverse. So the inverse graph is obtained by exchanging the coordinates of every point, and exchanging the coordinates is precisely reflection in the line y = x. This is also why the two graphs always cross on that line: any intersection there is a pair (c, c) with f(c) = c, a fixed point of f.

questions.explanation: The two graphs are mirror images because a point records an input and its output, and inverting the relation reverses which of the two is the input. Reflection in the line y equals x is exactly the operation of exchanging those two coordinates, so it converts the graph of f into the graph of the inverse. The same observation explains why the curves always intersect on the mirror line wherever f has a fixed point, and why the mirror line is the axis along which the two graphs are symmetric rather than merely similar.
questions.hint: Start from what the point (a, b) on the original graph asserts, then swap the two coordinates.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: apply the chain rule to the arcsine function
questions.stem: For a differentiable function u of x, what is the derivative of the arcsine of u of x? State the valid domain.

answer.exemplar: The derivative is u prime of x divided by the square root of 1 minus u of x squared. The domain restriction is that u of x must lie in the closed interval from minus 1 to 1, and at the two endpoints where u of x equals plus or minus 1 the square root in the denominator vanishes, so the derivative formula does not apply there. It follows by inverting y equals the sine of u, which gives u equals arcsine of y, differentiating both sides to obtain 1 equals u prime times the reciprocal of the square root of 1 minus u squared, and then solving for u prime.

questions.explanation: Start from y = sin u, which is the equation that defines u as a function of y, and read it as u = arcsin y. Differentiating with respect to y gives du/dy times the cosine of u equal to one, so du/dy = 1 over the cosine of u. The identity that the sine squared plus the cosine squared equals one then turns the cosine into the square root of one minus the sine squared, which is the square root of one minus u squared. The domain matters: u must stay inside the closed interval from minus 1 to 1, and at its two endpoints the cosine vanishes so the formula blows up.

The exponential of x plus the exponential of negative x, all divided by 2
options.misconception: quotes the definition of the hyperbolic cosine, which is the plus version of the same pair

options.text: The sine of x with x replaced by the exponential of x inside the argument
options.misconception: believes the hyperbolic functions are just trigonometric ones composed with an exponential

options.text: The difference of the cosine of x and the cosine of negative x, all divided by 2
options.misconception: mixes a difference with the cosine, which does not even have the odd parity the definition needs

questions.explanation: The hyperbolic sine is built from exponentials the way the circular sine is built from trigonometric exponentials: the exponential of x minus the exponential of negative x, divided by 2. The minus sign is what gives it the odd parity the sine function has, since replacing x by minus x swaps the two exponentials and negates the result. The plus version, divided by 2, is by definition the hyperbolic cosine, and the ratio of the two is the hyperbolic tangent.
questions.hint: The hyperbolic functions are built from the exponential pair, one with a plus and one with a minus.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why the hyperbolic tangent stays strictly between minus one and one
questions.stem: Why does the hyperbolic tangent of x always lie strictly between minus one and one for real x?

options.text: Because the hyperbolic cosine always exceeds the hyperbolic sine in absolute value, so their ratio never reaches one
Because the exponential of x always exceeds the exponential of negative x for positive x only
options.misconception: restricts the comparison to positive x and so cannot explain the negative half of the line

options.text: Because the hyperbolic cosine is always at least 1, which bounds the denominator from below but not the ratio
options.misconception: believes a bound on the denominator alone bounds the quotient, ignoring the numerator

options.text: Because the hyperbolic tangent is periodic, and any periodic function is bounded on a closed interval
options.misconception: assumes boundedness from periodicity, although the hyperbolic tangent is not periodic at all

questions.explanation: The identity that the square of the hyperbolic cosine minus the square of the hyperbolic sine equals 1 forces the hyperbolic cosine to be larger in absolute value than the hyperbolic sine, for every real x. A ratio whose denominator always dominates in absolute value has magnitude strictly less than one, and the sign of the ratio follows the sign of the sine. The hyperbolic tangent is not periodic at all, and the fact that the cosine is at least 1 is not by itself enough, since a large denominator says nothing unless the numerator is also controlled.
questions.hint: Use the identity cosh squared minus sinh squared equals 1 to compare the two magnitudes.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the hyperbolic functions numerically from their exponential definitions
questions.stem: Using the exponential definitions, what is the value of the hyperbolic tangent of 1? Give your answer to six decimal places.
questions.explanation: The definition of the hyperbolic tangent is the ratio of the exponential pair with a minus over the same pair with a plus, so at x = 1 it is the exponential of 2 minus 1 over the exponential of 2 plus 1, that is (7.389056 - 1) over (7.389056 + 1). The numerator is 6.389056 and the denominator is 8.389056, and the ratio is 0.761594. The independent route divides the two values directly: the hyperbolic sine of 1 is 1.175201 and the hyperbolic cosine of 1 is 1.543081, and 1.175201 over 1.543081 is again 0.761594.
questions.hint: Write the tangent as (e to the 2x minus 1) over (e to the 2x plus 1) at x = 1.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: The identity cosh squared minus sinh squared
questions.learningObjective: state the fundamental identity satisfied by the hyperbolic functions
questions.stem: Which identity is satisfied by the hyperbolic sine and the hyperbolic cosine for every real x?

options.text: The square of the hyperbolic cosine minus the square of the hyperbolic sine equals 1
The square of the hyperbolic cosine plus the square of the hyperbolic sine equals 1
options.misconception: quotes the circular identity for sine and cosine, which does not hold for the hyperbolic pair

options.text: The square of the hyperbolic sine plus the square of the hyperbolic cosine equals 1
options.misconception: arranges the two terms in the wrong order, which changes the value from 1 to 2 cosh squared

options.text: The product of the hyperbolic sine and the hyperbolic cosine equals 1
options.misconception: conflates the product with the difference of the two squares

questions.explanation: Substituting the exponential definitions and multiplying out leaves exactly 1, because the cross terms cancel and the surviving exponentials combine, so the square of the hyperbolic cosine minus the square of the hyperbolic sine equals 1 for every real x. The order of the two terms matters: reversing them would give the sum, which equals twice the square of the hyperbolic cosine and grows without bound. The minus sign is exactly what distinguishes this identity from the familiar circular one.
questions.hint: Expand the exponential definitions and watch the cross terms cancel.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: The identity cosh squared minus sinh squared
questions.learningObjective: verify a hyperbolic identity by differentiating it
questions.stem: Describe how differentiating the expression that is the square of the hyperbolic cosine minus the square of the hyperbolic sine confirms the identity.

answer.exemplar: Differentiating gives 2 cosh x sinh x minus 2 sinh x cosh x, which is identically zero, so the expression is a constant. Evaluating that constant at x = 0 gives 1 squared minus 0 squared, which is 1, so the expression equals 1 everywhere. The same two rules that produce the cancellation, namely the derivative of the hyperbolic sine is the hyperbolic cosine and the derivative of the hyperbolic cosine is the hyperbolic sine, are the mirror image of the circular rules with no minus sign, which is why the cancellation is exact.

questions.explanation: A useful check on any proposed identity is to differentiate it: if the derivative is identically zero then the expression is a constant, and a single evaluation pins the constant down. Here the derivative is 2 cosh sinh minus 2 sinh cosh, which is exactly zero term for term, so the expression is constant; evaluating at x = 0 gives 1 minus 0, so the constant is 1. The absence of a minus sign in the hyperbolic derivative pair, unlike the circular pair, is precisely what allows the products to match rather than to reinforce.
questions.hint: Differentiate both terms and look for identical products with opposite signs.

questions.topic: The identity cosh squared minus sinh squared
questions.learningObjective: use the hyperbolic identity to compute the hyperbolic tangent from given components
questions.stem: Suppose the hyperbolic sine of x is 3/4 and the hyperbolic cosine of x is 5/4. What is the value of the hyperbolic tangent of x?
questions.explanation: The hyperbolic tangent is the ratio of the hyperbolic sine to the hyperbolic cosine, so it is (3/4) over (5/4), which is 3 over 5, that is 0.6. The pair given is consistent, because 25 over 16 minus 9 over 16 equals 16 over 16, which is 1, exactly as the identity demands. An independent route uses the identity rewritten as the tangent squared equals 1 minus the reciprocal of the square of the hyperbolic cosine, giving a tangent of the square root of 1 minus 16 over 25, which is the square root of 9 over 25, again 3 over 5.
questions.hint: Divide the two given values, then confirm with the identity that the square of their difference is 1.

questions.topic: The identity cosh squared minus sinh squared
questions.learningObjective: invert the exponential definition to solve a hyperbolic cosine equation
questions.stem: The hyperbolic cosine of x is 5/4 and x is known to be positive. What is the value of x, as a decimal?
questions.explanation: From the definition, 5/4 equals the exponential of x plus the exponential of negative x, divided by 2, so putting u for the exponential of x gives u plus 1 over u equals 5 over 2. Multiplying through by u and by 2 gives 2u squared minus 5u plus 2, which factors as (2u - 1)(u - 2), so u is 2 or 1/2. Positivity of x selects u = 2, and the exponential of x equals 2 means x is the natural logarithm of 2, that is 0.693147. The independent route is to recognise the whole expression as the inverse hyperbolic cosine of 5 over 4, which agrees.
questions.hint: Put u for the exponential of x, solve the resulting quadratic, and take a logarithm.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: differentiate a scaled hyperbolic sine and read off the rate
questions.stem: A cable has length L of x equal to 4 cosh of x metres, where x is an angle in radians. If x increases at 0.5 radians per second, how fast is the length changing when x equals 1 radian?
questions.explanation: The length depends on time through x, so the rate of change of length is the derivative of L with respect to x multiplied by the rate of change of x. The derivative of 4 cosh of x is 4 sinh of x, and the hyperbolic sine of 1 is 1.175201, so at x = 1 that derivative is 4.700805 metres per radian. Multiplying by 0.5 radians per second gives 2.350402 metres per second. The units cancel correctly, leaving only metres per second, since radians are dimensionless.
questions.hint: Chain the rate of change through x: dL/dt equals dL/dx multiplied by dx/dt.

questions.learningObjective: differentiate the hyperbolic tangent of a composite argument
questions.stem: What is the value of the derivative of the hyperbolic tangent of x squared, at the point where x equals 1?
questions.explanation: The derivative of the hyperbolic tangent of a quantity is the reciprocal of the square of the hyperbolic cosine of that quantity, and here the chain rule contributes 2x as well. At x = 1 the factor 2x is 2, and the hyperbolic cosine of 1 is 1.543081, whose square is 2.381098, so the value is 2 over 2.381098, that is 0.839949. The same figure follows by differentiating the exponential form of the hyperbolic tangent directly, and the fact that the result is below 1 is consistent with the tangent itself never exceeding 1 in magnitude.
questions.hint: Use the reciprocal-square-cosine rule and multiply by the chain-rule factor 2x.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: match described graphs to the inverse hyperbolic functions
questions.stem: Three curves are sketched on one set of axes. Curve P starts at the point (0, 0), rises through the origin with slope 1, and grows without bound in both directions. Curve Q starts at the point (1, 0), is undefined for x below 1, and rises without bound to the right. Curve R is defined only for x strictly between minus 1 and 1, passes through the origin with slope 1, and climbs towards positive infinity as x approaches 1. Which curve is the inverse hyperbolic sine, which is the inverse hyperbolic cosine, and which is the inverse hyperbolic tangent?

options.text: Curve P is the inverse hyperbolic sine, Curve Q is the inverse hyperbolic cosine, Curve R is the inverse hyperbolic tangent
Curve P is the inverse hyperbolic cosine, Curve Q is the inverse hyperbolic sine, Curve R is the inverse hyperbolic tangent
options.misconception: swaps the two curves whose endpoints are (0, 0) and (1, 0), ignoring where each one is defined

options.text: Curve P is the inverse hyperbolic tangent, Curve Q is the inverse hyperbolic cosine, Curve R is the inverse hyperbolic sine
options.misconception: judges by the growth at the ends and ignores the endpoint from which the sine inverse starts

options.text: Curve P is the inverse hyperbolic sine, Curve Q is the inverse hyperbolic tangent, Curve R is the inverse hyperbolic cosine
options.misconception: believes the curve that blows up at x = 1 is the cosine inverse rather than the tangent inverse

questions.explanation: Each of these curves is the reflection in the line y equals x of the corresponding hyperbolic function, so the identifying feature is where the original is defined. The hyperbolic sine takes every real value once, so its inverse starts at the origin and is defined for all x, which is Curve P. The hyperbolic cosine takes values at least 1, so its inverse starts at (1, 0) and is undefined to the left of 1, which is Curve Q. The hyperbolic tangent takes values strictly between minus 1 and 1, so its inverse has two vertical asymptotes at plus and minus 1, which is Curve R.
questions.hint: The domain of each original function fixes where the reflected curve begins and where it blows up.

questions.learningObjective: differentiate a scaled inverse hyperbolic sine
questions.stem: What is the value of the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic sine of 2x, at the point where x equals 1?
questions.explanation: The derivative of the inverse hyperbolic sine of a quantity is the reciprocal of the square root of 1 plus the square of that quantity, and the chain rule contributes 2. At x = 1 the quantity is 2, so the denominator is the square root of 1 plus 4, that is the square root of 5, and the numerator is 2, giving 0.894427. The domain is all real numbers, so nothing restricts this point. A second route writes the derivative as the reciprocal of the hyperbolic cosine of the inverse value, and at the point in question that cosine is the square root of 5, again giving 0.894427.
questions.hint: The denominator is the square root of 1 plus the square of the argument, not 1 minus it.

options.text: The inverse hyperbolic cosine of 2, which equals 1.316958

questions.explanation: Compare the four values: 0.549306, 0.693147, 0.881374 and 1.316958. They are already in increasing order, so the arrangement is A, B, C, D. questions.hint: Write each value as a logarithm, then compare the arguments, remembering the logarithm is increasing.
